account: RL's weight change is 0.24 % of the weight norm, and about 12 % of its square sits in 8 input-to-output direction pairs per matrix (0.5-0.8 % for noise) whose inputs are directions the base's own text already drives strongly (8-11x a random subspace; code text drives Math's inputs 0.87 as much as math text); because RL trains on the model's own samples, every reward concentrates this way (top-8 share 0.12-0.21 for Math, Code, IF and LM-judge RL against 0.03 for Think-SFT, whose diffuse change still lies along the same base-driven inputs).

Added to the base, the pairs act as one graded shift on every sample, not a per-sample lottery: they switch the base into its own deliberate-then-commit mode (open with 'Okay', more hold-on words, finish and state the answer in the task's format) and make its scattered slips rarer on problems it can already solve, so the 1.5x edit matches RL (MATH-500 456 vs 457, hard328 200.25 vs 200.0) and even its short answers are right.

The base already contains the switch: a 3-token opening, its own 'Okay' openings drawn at T 1.0, or a one-tensor hand edit turn it on per prompt (MATH-500 224 to 410, RL 463), which is about what the first 100 RL steps learn, still incompletely (step 100 plain 418 with the cued base's cap-hit rate, and the cue still adds 8.5), giving about 78 % of RL's gain on MATH-500 and 53-77 % on code and general questions.

What remains is reliability: 81 % of the MATH-500 gap lies on problems the base solves in at least 1 of 4 samples, and its wrong answers there are split slips (same-problem wrong pairs agree 26 %, not one attractor value), so a plurality vote over about 6 cued samples recovers it (456.6 against one RL sample's 456-463).

Inference cannot add solves the base never samples: on hard328 the vote only narrows the gap (195 vs 224) because the base has no right sample within the 16,384-token cap on 26 of RL's 36 vote wins, at T 0.6 the switched base loops instead (52-63 % of its answers past 4,096 tokens), and a 4,096 cap cuts its right routes, which are longer.

The pairs carry the shared shift, not RL's problem-specific choices: Code-RL's pairs raise code correctness where Math's barely do (the output side is reward-specific although the inputs are driven by any text), the edit's code fixes are problems the base solves in other samples, and on problems RL fails but the base passes the edit passes at the base's own resample rate.

consequences.claim: If on-policy RL under any reward concentrates in the inputs the base's own text drives (S1), Code-RL 3.1's change must sit in RL-Math 3.1's top-8 input subspace far more than off-policy Think-SFT's diffuse change does. If each reward wrote its own subspace, Code's capture would be no higher than Think-SFT's.
consequences.why_new: F24 gives only Think-SFT's capture (4.80x chance) and says the >=2x property is 'shared' with Code 3.1; no fact or result gives Code 3.1's capture relative to Think-SFT's in the same subspace.
consequences.statistic: median over matrices of cap_right(Code 3.1 change, Math 3.1 top-8 input subspace) / cap_right(Think-SFT change, same subspace), a ratio (unitless)
consequences.rows: all 224 layer matrices (32 layers x q,k,v,o,gate,up,down), entries cap_right of Code 3.1 and of Think-SFT against the RL-Math 3.1 top-8 right (input) subspace
consequences.computation: 1) For each matrix read cap_right for Code 3.1 and for Think-SFT against the Math 3.1 top-8 input subspace. 2) Per matrix ratio r = Code / Think-SFT. 3) Statistic = median of r over the 224 matrices. 4) 90 % interval: resample the 224 matrices with replacement 10,000 times, take the median each time, report the 5th and 95th percentiles.
consequences.null: Another model's change in the same subspace: Think-SFT's own capture, so ratio about 1 if concentration is reward-specific and Code's change is as unrelated to Math's inputs as a diffuse fine-tune

consequences.claim: If concentration is set by which base inputs the model's own samples drive (S1), the matrices where Math-RL concentrates most should also be the ones where an unrelated on-policy reward (IF) concentrates most, beyond what they share with off-policy Think-SFT.
consequences.why_new: F03 and result-82eb02 compare mean top-8 shares across models only. No fact or result relates the per-matrix concentration pattern of one reward to another's.
consequences.statistic: Spearman rho(Math 3.1, IF) minus Spearman rho(Math 3.1, Think-SFT) of per-matrix top-8 share after each module family's median is subtracted (difference of correlations, unitless)
consequences.rows: all 224 matrices; keys RL-Zero-Math 3.1, RL-Zero-IF and Think-SFT
consequences.computation: 1) For each key, subtract from each matrix's top-8 share the median share of its module family (q,k,v,o,gate,up,down) over 32 layers, which removes shape effects. 2) Spearman rho over the 224 matrices of Math 3.1 vs IF residuals, and of Math 3.1 vs Think-SFT residuals. 3) Statistic = difference. 4) 90 % interval: resample matrices with replacement 10,000 times (the same draw for both rhos), recompute the difference, take the 5th and 95th percentiles.
consequences.null: Another model's directions: Think-SFT's per-matrix pattern shares as much with Math-RL as IF-RL does, so the difference is about 0 (concentration pattern reward- or training-agnostic)

consequences.claim: If the 1.5x top-8 edit carries RL's shared shift but not its problem-specific choices (S6), then on hard328 problems where RL solves none of 4 samples the edit keeps at least most of the base's right answers, as F20 found on code. If the edit copied RL's outcomes, it would lose them.
consequences.why_new: F19/F20 test this only on code. No fact or listed result splits the hard328 edit rows by RL's per-problem outcome.
consequences.statistic: edit right samples / base right samples on hard328 problems with RL 0 of 4 right (ratio, unitless)
consequences.rows: problems whose RL plain attempt-0 samples 0-3 are all wrong (grader v3); on them the 4 edit samples and the base's attempt-0 samples 0-3 (restarts excluded); problems missing any of the 12 rows dropped
consequences.computation: 1) From RL rows pick problems with 0 of 4 right (attempt 0). 2) On those, E = right edit samples and B = right base samples (attempt 0, samples 0-3), both grader v3. 3) Statistic = E / B. 4) 90 % interval: resample the selected problems with replacement 10,000 times, recompute E/B, take the 5th and 95th percentiles. n = 4 x number of selected problems (edit rows).
consequences.null: The edit copies RL's outcomes per problem (fully or for two thirds of samples), so edit right samples on RL-0/4 problems fall to at most half the base's
